statement: In the Merton model, equity is a call option on the firm's assets with strike price equal to the face value of the debt, and the value of the debt equals asset value minus equity value.
explanation: Shareholders hold a call on the firm's assets struck at the debt's face value, and creditors own the remainder of the assets. Debt value is therefore the asset value minus the equity value.
originalText: Equity is a call option on the firm’s assets with strike price equal to the face value of the debt, and debt value equals asset value minus equity value.

statement: In the Merton model, equity is a put option on the firm's assets with strike price equal to the face value of the debt.
explanation: Equity is a call option on the firm's assets, not a put. The put is the creditors' short position (the default option), not the equity payoff.
originalText: Equity is a put option on the firm’s assets with strike price equal to the face value of the debt.
correction: In the Merton model, equity is a call option on the firm's assets with strike price equal to the face value of the debt.

statement: In the Merton model, the value of the debt equals the asset value plus the equity value.
explanation: Assets are the sum of debt and equity, so the debt value equals the asset value minus the equity value.
originalText: Debt value equals asset value plus equity value.
correction: In the Merton model, the value of the debt equals the asset value minus the equity value.

statement: In the Merton model, equity value is unaffected by the volatility of firm assets because the debt is fixed.
explanation: Equity is a call option on the firm's assets, and a call's value rises with the volatility of the underlying. Higher asset volatility therefore increases equity value even though the debt's face value is fixed.
originalText: Equity value is unaffected by the volatility of firm assets because the debt is fixed.
correction: In the Merton model, equity value increases with the volatility of firm assets because equity is a call option on those assets.

changes.to: equity is a call option on those assets

statement: In the Merton model with a single zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a higher asset volatility, all else equal, increases the value of the firm's equity.
explanation: Equity is a call option on the firm's assets, and a call has positive vega, so higher asset volatility raises its value.
originalText: A higher asset volatility increases the value of the firm’s equity.

statement: In the Merton model with a single zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a higher asset volatility, all else equal, decreases the value of the firm's debt.
explanation: Debt equals asset value minus equity value. With asset value fixed and equity rising with volatility, debt falls, because the embedded short put on the assets is worth more.
originalText: A higher asset volatility decreases the value of the firm’s debt.

statement: In the Merton model with a single zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, equity value decreases as the debt's time to maturity approaches zero, all else equal.
explanation: With less time left, the equity call loses time value, so equity value falls toward the asset value minus the face value of the debt.
originalText: As the debt’s time to maturity $T \to0$, the value of the firm’s equity decreases.

statement: In the Merton model with a single zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, debt value decreases as the debt's time to maturity approaches zero, all else equal.
explanation: As maturity shrinks, the equity call loses time value, so the residual debt claim (assets minus equity) rises toward par. The embedded short put on the assets loses time value, which raises debt value.
originalText: As the debt’s time to maturity $T \to0$, the value of the firm’s debt decreases.
correction: In the Merton model with a single zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, debt value increases as the debt's time to maturity approaches zero, all else equal.

statement: In the Merton model, a fall in the riskless interest rate increases the value of equity, holding firm value, asset volatility and maturities unchanged.
explanation: Equity is a call option on the firm's assets, and a call loses value as the riskless rate falls. With firm value fixed, the value lost by equity passes to the debt holders.
originalText: The value of equity increases.
correction: In the Merton model, a fall in the riskless interest rate decreases the value of equity, holding firm value, asset volatility and maturities unchanged.

statement: In the Merton model, a fall in the riskless interest rate decreases the value of senior debt, holding firm value, asset volatility and maturities unchanged.
explanation: Senior debt equals firm value minus a call on the firm's assets struck at the senior face value. A lower riskless rate reduces that call's value, so senior debt value rises.
originalText: The value of the senior debt decreases.
correction: In the Merton model, a fall in the riskless interest rate increases the value of senior debt, holding firm value, asset volatility and maturities unchanged.

statement: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, an increase in the volatility of the firm's assets decreases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.
explanation: Debt holders are effectively short a put on the firm's assets. Higher volatility raises the value of that option, transferring value from debt holders to equity holders.
originalText: An increase in the volatility of the firm’s assets

statement: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a decrease in the risk-free interest rate decreases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.
explanation: A lower risk-free rate reduces the value of the equity call, leaving more of the firm's value for the debt, so debt value rises.
originalText: A decrease in the risk‑free interest rate
correction: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a decrease in the risk-free interest rate increases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.

statement: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a shorter time to maturity of the debt decreases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.
explanation: As maturity shortens, the embedded short put loses time value and the equity call loses value, so the debt is pulled up toward par.
originalText: A shorter time to maturity of the debt
correction: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, a shorter time to maturity of the debt increases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.

statement: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, an increase in the current value of the firm's assets decreases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.
explanation: More assets make the debt safer, because the embedded put on the assets is further out of the money. Debt value therefore rises when asset value rises.
originalText: An increase in the current value of the firm’s assets
correction: In the Merton model with a zero-coupon bond and firm assets worth more than the bond's face value, an increase in the current value of the firm's assets increases the value of the firm's debt, other inputs constant.

statement: In the Merton model, the distance to default measures the number of standard deviations by which the firm's asset value must change for default to occur at the debt's maturity.
explanation: Distance to default (equal to $d_2$) standardises the cushion between the asset value and the default point by asset volatility, so it is expressed in standard deviations. A larger distance means a lower default probability.
originalText: The number of standard deviations by which the firm’s asset value must change for default to occur at the debt’s maturity.

statement: In the Merton model, the distance to default measures the difference between a firm's total assets and total liabilities.
explanation: An absolute asset-minus-liability gap is not scaled by volatility. Distance to default is the cushion expressed in standard deviations of asset value.
originalText: The difference between a firm’s total assets and total liabilities.

statement: In the Merton model, the distance to default measures the gap between the market value of equity and the face value of debt.
explanation: Equity minus debt is an absolute currency gap. Distance to default is volatility-scaled and measured in standard deviations.
originalText: The gap between the market value of equity and the face value of debt.

statement: In the Merton model, the distance to default measures the time remaining until the firm's debt reaches maturity.
explanation: Time to maturity is an input to $d_2$, not what $d_2$ measures. Distance to default is a number of standard deviations.
originalText: The time remaining until the firm’s debt reaches maturity.

statement: Vasicek's Gaussian copula model is used to calculate the high-percentile default rates that determine regulatory capital under the Basel II internal-ratings-based approach.
explanation: Vasicek's one-factor Gaussian copula model gives the worst-case default rate from the PD, the correlation and the confidence level, which is the building block of IRB capital.
originalText: Vasicek’s Gaussian copula model

statement: CreditMetrics with Monte Carlo simulation is the model used to calculate the high-percentile default rates that determine regulatory capital under the Basel II internal-ratings-based approach.
explanation: CreditMetrics models rating migrations by simulation and is an internal credit VaR approach. The IRB capital formula is based on Vasicek's Gaussian copula model.
originalText: CreditMetrics with Monte Carlo simulation

statement: CreditRisk+ is the model used to calculate the high-percentile default rates that determine regulatory capital under the Basel II internal-ratings-based approach.
explanation: CreditRisk+ is an insurance-style Poisson default model used for internal credit VaR. The IRB regulatory formula is based on Vasicek's Gaussian copula model.
originalText: CreditRisk+

statement: In Vasicek's model for Basel II IRB capital, a higher credit correlation $\rho$ raises the capital requirement, since defaults are more likely to occur simultaneously.
explanation: Higher correlation means less diversification and a fatter tail of joint defaults. The 99.9% worst-case default rate, and hence capital, therefore increases.
originalText: A higher $\rho$ raises capital, since defaults are more likely to occur simultaneously.

statement: In Vasicek's model for Basel II IRB capital, a higher credit correlation $\rho$ lowers the capital requirement, since defaults are more diversified across the portfolio.
explanation: Higher correlation means less diversification, not more. It raises the worst-case default rate and therefore capital.
originalText: A higher $\rho$ lowers capital, since defaults are more diversified across the portfolio.
correction: In Vasicek's model for Basel II IRB capital, a higher credit correlation $\rho$ raises the capital requirement, since defaults are less diversified across the portfolio.

statement: In Vasicek's model for Basel II IRB capital, a higher credit correlation $\rho$ lowers the capital requirement, since it implies better management of default risk.
explanation: Correlation is not a measure of management quality. A higher $\rho$ raises the worst-case default rate and therefore raises capital.
originalText: A higher $\rho$ lowers capital, since it implies better management of default risk.

statement: In Vasicek's model for Basel II IRB capital, a lower credit correlation $\rho$ raises the capital requirement, since default patterns are less predictable.
explanation: The direction is reversed: a lower $\rho$ reduces the worst-case default rate and therefore reduces capital.
originalText: A lower $\rho$ raises capital, since default patterns are less predictable.

statement: In Vasicek's model, the confidence level X determines the worst-case default rate that the bank must be able to withstand.
explanation: The confidence level selects the percentile of the default rate distribution that defines the worst-case default rate WCDR(T, X).
originalText: It determines the worst‑case default rate the bank must be able to withstand.

statement: In Vasicek's model, the confidence level X sets the expected loss that the capital allocation must cover.
explanation: Expected loss depends on PD, LGD and EAD only. The confidence level concerns the tail of the loss distribution beyond expected loss.
originalText: It sets the expected loss the capital allocation must cover.

statement: In Vasicek's model, the confidence level X dictates the degree of diversification that the loan portfolio must achieve.
explanation: Diversification is reflected in the correlation parameter $\rho$, not in X. The confidence level only selects the percentile of the default rate distribution.
originalText: It dictates the degree of diversification the loan portfolio must achieve.

statement: Recomputing the worst-case default rate from Vasicek's model requires the probability of default, the credit correlation and the confidence level.
explanation: The Vasicek formula is fully determined by the PD, the correlation and the confidence level (plus the time horizon). Back-tests and macroeconomic scenarios are not needed to recompute it.
originalText: The probability of default, the credit correlation, the confidence level, and how the first two were estimated.

statement: In Vasicek's model, at $\rho = 0$ the worst-case default rate equals the PD, and it rises as the correlation $\rho$ increases because defaults become more clustered in the tail.
explanation: With $\rho = 0$ defaults are independent and a large portfolio's default rate converges to the PD. Correlation adds the positive term $\sqrt{\rho}N^{-1}(X)$, which raises the tail default rate.
originalText: At $\rho= 0$ the worst‑case default rate equals the PD, and it rises as $\rho$ increases because defaults become more clustered in the tail.

statement: In Vasicek's model, the worst-case default rate falls as the correlation $\rho$ increases because higher correlation means greater diversification.
explanation: Higher correlation reduces diversification, so tail defaults and the worst-case default rate increase.
originalText: The worst‑case default rate falls as $\rho$ increases because higher correlation means greater diversification.
correction: In Vasicek's model, the worst-case default rate rises as the correlation $\rho$ increases because higher correlation means less diversification.

statement: In Vasicek's model, at $\rho = 0$ the worst-case default rate is already far above the PD because the confidence level X is so high.
explanation: With no correlation the $N^{-1}(X)$ term vanishes, so X has no effect and the worst-case default rate equals the PD.
originalText: At $\rho= 0$ the worst‑case default rate is already far above the PD because X is so high.
correction: In Vasicek's model, at $\rho = 0$ the worst-case default rate equals the PD, however high the confidence level X is.

changes.from: is already far above the PD because the confidence level X is so high
changes.to: equals the PD, however high the confidence level X is

statement: In Vasicek's model, once the confidence level X is fixed at 99.9%, the worst-case default rate no longer depends on the correlation $\rho$.
explanation: $\rho$ enters both the numerator and the denominator of the formula, so the worst-case default rate changes with $\rho$ at any X.
originalText: Once X is fixed at 99.9%, the worst‑case default rate no longer depends on $\rho$.

statement: In Vasicek's Gaussian copula model, the Xth percentile loss for a large portfolio of small loans is approximated by $\sum_{i} \text{WCDR}_{i}(T, X) \times \text{EAD}_{i} \times \text{LGD}_{i}$.
explanation: Gordy's result extends the single-loan formula to a large portfolio of small loans as the sum of each loan's worst-case default rate times its EAD and LGD.
originalText: The Xth percentile loss for a large portfolio of small loans is approximated by $\sum_{i} \text{WCDR}_{i}(T, X) \times\text{EAD}_{i} \times\text{LGD}_{i}$.

statement: In Vasicek's Gaussian copula model, the credit correlation $\rho$ can be estimated from the average correlation between equity returns of the companies in the portfolio, or of similar publicly traded companies if they are private.
explanation: Structural models make $ho$ the correlation of asset returns, and equity-return correlation is the practical proxy for it.
originalText: The credit correlation $\rho$ can be estimated from the average correlation between equity returns of the companies in the portfolio (or of similar publicly traded companies if they are private).

statement: For regulatory capital under Vasicek's model, the sum of loan-level worst-case losses is evaluated with a one-year horizon and a 99.9% confidence level.
explanation: The Basel IRB regulatory parameters are T = 1 year and X = 99.9%.
originalText: For regulatory capital the sum is evaluated with T = one year and X = 99.9%.

statement: Vasicek's Gaussian copula model is used to set the interest rate charged on new loans by assessing the portfolio's expected profit.
explanation: The model estimates a worst-case loss percentile and hence regulatory capital. It is not a loan-pricing model.
originalText: The model is used to set the interest rate charged on new loans by assessing the portfolio’s expected profit.

statement: Exercising a break clause gives the exercising party the authority to terminate the transaction at its current replacement value.
explanation: A break clause lets a party close the trade at its prevailing replacement (market) value at the time of termination, so it can exit when the counterparty's credit quality weakens.
originalText: The exercising party will have the authority to terminate the transaction at its current replacement value.

statement: Exercising a break clause gives the exercising party the authority to terminate the transaction at a pre-defined replacement value.
explanation: Termination is settled at the replacement value at the time of termination, not at a value fixed in advance.
originalText: The exercising party will have authority to terminate the transaction at its pre‑defined replacement value.
correction: Exercising a break clause gives the exercising party the authority to terminate the transaction at its current replacement value.

statement: Exercising a break clause gives the defaulting party the authority to terminate the transaction at its current replacement value.
explanation: The right belongs to the party exercising the clause, typically the one concerned about the counterparty's credit quality, not specifically to a defaulting party.
originalText: The defaulting party will have authority to terminate the transaction at its current replacement value.

statement: A mandatory break clause means the transaction will certainly terminate at the date of the break clause, regardless of the financial situations of both parties.
explanation: A mandatory break clause terminates the trade automatically on the specified date, irrespective of either party's credit condition and with no discretion.
originalText: the transaction will certainly terminate at the date of the break clause regardless of the financial situations of both parties.

statement: A mandatory break clause means the transaction will not terminate at the date of the break clause, regardless of the situations of both parties.
explanation: A mandatory break clause does the opposite: the trade does terminate on the specified date.
originalText: the transaction will not terminate at the date of the break clause regardless of the situations of both parties.
correction: A mandatory break clause means the transaction will terminate at the date of the break clause, regardless of the situations of both parties.

statement: A mandatory break clause gives both parties the option to terminate the trade depending on the creditworthiness of each party.
explanation: That describes an optional break clause, where a party chooses whether to terminate. A mandatory clause leaves no discretion.
originalText: both parties have the option to terminate the trade transaction depending on the creditworthiness of each party.

statement: A mandatory break clause means the transaction will certainly terminate at the date of the break clause but gives the defaulting party an option to accept or reject it.
explanation: A mandatory break clause gives no accept-or-reject choice to either party. The trade terminates on the date.
originalText: the transaction will certainly terminate at the date of the break clause but give the defaulting party an option to accept it or reject it.

statement: A break clause is most useful if exercised early, before the counterparty's credit quality deteriorates substantially, but firms often avoid early exercise to preserve relationships with counterparties.
explanation: This is the banker's paradox: a break clause is most valuable when exercised early, yet institutions avoid exercising it to keep good relationships.
originalText: A break clause is most useful if exercised early, before the counterparty’s credit quality deteriorates substantially, but firms often avoid early exercise to preserve relationships with counterparties.

statement: A walkaway clause allows a party to avoid its net liabilities to a defaulted counterparty while still claiming if its own mark-to-market exposure is positive, and it is criticised for creating moral hazard.
explanation: A walkaway clause lets the non-defaulting party escape net liabilities to a defaulter while still claiming on positive MtM. It is criticised for moral hazard.
originalText: A walkaway clause allows a party to avoid its net liabilities to a defaulted counterparty while still claiming if its own MtM exposure is positive, and it is criticised for creating moral hazard.

statement: A reset agreement resets a trade that is heavily in the money back to at the money, for example by exchanging the mark-to-market value on each reset date.
explanation: Resetting exchanges accumulated MtM and returns the trade to at the money, as in a resettable cross-currency swap whose FX rate is reset on each reset date.
originalText: A reset agreement resets a trade that is heavily in the money back to at the money, for example by exchanging the MtM value on each reset date.

statement: Trade compression reduces the gross notional and the number of trades, but it can do so only by changing the institution's overall risk profile.
explanation: Trade compression nets redundant trades to cut gross notional and trade count while leaving the institution's overall risk profile unchanged.
originalText: Trade compression reduces the gross notional and the number of trades, but it can do so only by changing the institution’s overall risk profile.
correction: Trade compression reduces the gross notional and the number of trades without changing the institution's overall risk profile.

changes.from: but it can do so only by changing

statement: A credit support annex typically specifies the eligible collateral and the haircuts applied to non-cash collateral.
explanation: Eligible collateral and haircuts are core collateral terms set in the CSA.
originalText: The eligible collateral and the haircuts applied to non‑cash collateral

statement: A credit support annex typically sets the threshold, the independent amount (initial margin) and the minimum transfer amount.
explanation: These are the core credit support parameters that a CSA defines.
originalText: The threshold, independent amount (initial margin) and minimum transfer amount

statement: A credit support annex typically sets the method and timing of valuations and margin transfers, and the procedure for resolving disputes.
explanation: Valuation and transfer mechanics, and dispute resolution procedures, are explicit CSA terms.
originalText: The method and timing of valuations and of margin transfers, and the procedure for resolving disputes

statement: A credit support annex typically establishes the events of default and termination events that permit close-out netting of the trades.
explanation: The CSA is the collateral annex. Events of default, termination events and close-out netting are defined in the ISDA Master Agreement itself.
originalText: The events of default and termination events that permit close‑out netting of the trades

statement: A threshold in a CSA is the level of mark-to-market exposure below which no margin can be called, so only the exposure above it can be collateralised.
explanation: A threshold permits uncollateralised exposure up to a limit, which reduces operational and liquidity burden at the cost of weaker risk reduction. For example, with a USD 10 million threshold and USD 25 million exposure, only USD 15 million can be called.
originalText: It is the level of mark‑to‑market exposure below which no margin can be called; if exposure is \$25 million, only \$15 million can be called.

statement: In a CSA, the threshold is the minimum size of a single collateral transfer, below which no transfer is made.
explanation: That describes the minimum transfer amount (MTA), not the threshold.
originalText: It is the minimum size of a single collateral transfer, below which no transfer is made.
correction: In a CSA, the minimum transfer amount is the minimum size of a single collateral transfer, below which no transfer is made.

statement: In a CSA, the threshold is an extra amount of collateral that must be posted regardless of the portfolio value.
explanation: That describes initial margin (the independent amount). A threshold works in the opposite direction, subtracting from the amount that can be called.
originalText: It is an extra amount of collateral that must be posted regardless of the portfolio value, so a \$25 million exposure requires \$35 million.
correction: In a CSA, the initial margin is an extra amount of collateral that must be posted regardless of the portfolio value.

statement: In a CSA, the threshold is the level of mark-to-market exposure above which posted collateral must be liquidated.
explanation: A threshold governs when margin can be called, not when collateral is liquidated.
originalText: It is the level of mark‑to‑market exposure above which posted collateral must be liquidated.

statement: In a CSA, a threshold and initial margin (independent amount) work in opposite directions: a threshold allows undercollateralisation, while initial margin creates overcollateralisation.
explanation: The credit support amount is max(V minus threshold, 0) plus initial margin. A higher threshold reduces collateral called and a higher initial margin increases it, so initial margin behaves like a negative threshold.
originalText: They work in opposite directions: a threshold allows undercollateralisation, while initial margin creates overcollateralisation.

statement: In a CSA, a threshold and initial margin (independent amount) move in the same direction: both increase the collateral called.
explanation: The threshold subtracts from the amount called, while initial margin adds to it.
originalText: They move in the same direction: both increase the collateral called.
correction: In a CSA, a threshold and initial margin (independent amount) move in opposite directions: the threshold decreases and initial margin increases the collateral called.

changes.from: move in the same direction: both increase the collateral called
changes.to: move in opposite directions: the threshold decreases and initial margin increases the collateral called

statement: In a CSA, the threshold and the initial margin (independent amount) are always equal for a given counterparty.
explanation: No requirement links their sizes, and in practice usually one of them is zero.
originalText: They are always equal for a given counterparty.

statement: Under a CSA, a security posted as collateral with a haircut of 4% is credited at USD 0.96 for each USD 1 of its market value.
explanation: A haircut discounts the collateral's value, so the credit given equals (1 minus haircut) times market value. To meet a USD 1 call the poster must deliver 1/0.96, about USD 1.04, of the security.
originalText: For each \$1 of the security posted, the recipient gives credit of \$0.96.

statement: Under a CSA, a security posted as collateral with a haircut of 4% is credited at about USD 1.04 for each USD 1 of its market value.
explanation: The haircut reduces the credit given, so it is below market value: (1 minus 0.04) times market value is USD 0.96 per USD 1 posted.
originalText: For each \$1 of the security posted, the recipient gives credit of about \$1.04.
correction: Under a CSA, a security posted as collateral with a haircut of 4% is credited at USD 0.96 for each USD 1 of its market value.

statement: A credit support annex creates an obligation for the trading parties to post collateral as they have mutually agreed.
explanation: A CSA turns collateral posting into a contractual agreement appended to the ISDA Master Agreement, which mitigates counterparty credit risk.
originalText: To create an obligation for trading parties to mutually agree on posting collateral.

statement: The purpose of a credit support annex is to provide a mechanism for netting and settlement of trades.
explanation: Netting and settlement come from the ISDA Master Agreement. The CSA deals with collateral.
originalText: To provide a mechanism for netting and settlement of trades.

statement: The purpose of a credit support annex is to ensure that all derivative contracts are honored by both parties.
explanation: A CSA does not guarantee performance. It only provides collateral support that mitigates counterparty credit risk.
originalText: To ensure that all derivative contracts are honored by both parties involved.

statement: A credit support annex specifies the collateral terms, including events that trigger changes in collateral requirements.
explanation: A CSA is a flexible, negotiated agreement that sets the collateral terms, including changes triggered by events such as a rating downgrade.
originalText: It specifies the collateral terms, including events that trigger changes in collateral requirements.

statement: A credit support annex mandates a fixed collateral amount for the duration of all derivative contracts.
explanation: Collateral is recalculated regularly as the portfolio value changes. It is not fixed.
originalText: It mandates a fixed collateral amount for the duration of all derivative contracts.

statement: A credit support annex requires collateral to be posted exclusively in the form of government securities.
explanation: Eligible collateral is negotiated, and cash is the most common form. Various securities can also be eligible.
originalText: It requires collateral to be posted exclusively in the form of government securities.

statement: A credit support annex requires the same threshold to apply to both parties regardless of their credit quality.
explanation: Thresholds can differ by party and can be linked to credit quality, so they may be asymmetric.
originalText: It requires the same threshold to apply to both parties regardless of their credit quality.

statement: Collateral with higher price volatility, ceteris paribus, is assigned a higher haircut.
explanation: Haircuts are driven by the volatility and liquidity of the collateral, so more volatile collateral gets a larger haircut.
originalText: Collateral with higher price volatility, ceteris paribus, will be assigned a higher haircut

statement: A party that has already posted an independent amount (initial margin) can apply it against a variation margin call, so that it needs to deliver only the remainder.
explanation: The independent amount is overcollateralisation held separately and is not netted against the variation margin call. The party must still deliver the full variation margin.
originalText: If FundCorp has already posted an Independent Amount (IA) of \$60,000, then FundCorp can apply the IA and meet the margin call with only \$40,000

statement: A CSA is appended within an ISDA Master Agreement and permits the counterparties to mitigate their credit risk by agreeing to various collateral posting arrangements.
explanation: The CSA is an annex to the ISDA Master Agreement that provides for collateral posting.
originalText: A CSA is appended within an ISDA Master Agreement and permits the counterparties to mitigate their credit risk by agreeing to various collateral posting

statement: A CSA is critically defined by key parameters, including the threshold, the independent amount and the minimum transfer amount.
explanation: Threshold, independent amount (initial margin) and minimum transfer amount are key CSA parameters.
originalText: A CSA is critically defined by key parameters, including threshold, independent amount, and minimum transfer amount

statement: In some trading relationships CSAs are not used, because one or both parties cannot commit to collateral posting.
explanation: Entities that cannot post collateral, such as many corporates, often have no CSA.
originalText: In some trading relationships, CSAs are not used because one or both parties cannot commit to collateral posting

statement: If a counterparty employs a credit value adjustment (CVA), then a CSA gives no benefit and is not necessary.
explanation: CVA prices the expected loss from counterparty risk, while a CSA reduces the exposure itself, and so reduces the CVA charge. The two complement each other.
originalText: If a counterparty employs a credit value adjustment (CVA), then a CSA gives no benefit and is not necessary (a CSA would be redundant with CVA)

statement: ISDA documentation has helped standardize collateral management.
explanation: Collateral management moved from no legal standards to highly standardized practice through ISDA documentation introduced in 1994.

statement: CSAs must define all collateralization parameters in order to work as intended.
explanation: A CSA must define every collateralization parameter and account for the relevant scenarios in order to work as intended.

statement: CSAs are incorporated into an ISDA Master Agreement.
explanation: A CSA is an annex incorporated into the ISDA Master Agreement, not a separate stand-alone agreement.

statement: Compared to the ISDA Master Agreement, CSAs were first to establish collateral standards.
explanation: The CSA is an annex to the ISDA Master Agreement, so the ISDA framework came first and the CSA did not precede it as a standard-setter.

statement: Funding and capital costs, central clearing and bilateral margin requirements are pushing collateral thresholds increasingly toward zero.
explanation: These pressures remove the benefit of leaving exposure uncollateralised, so thresholds are increasingly zero. Two-way CSAs with zero thresholds are standard between financial counterparties.
originalText: Thresholds are increasingly set to zero

statement: Funding and capital costs, central clearing and bilateral margin requirements are pushing collateral thresholds increasingly toward infinity.
explanation: An infinite threshold means a party never posts margin, as in a one-way CSA. That is the opposite of the trend toward more margining.
originalText: Thresholds are increasingly set to infinity
correction: Funding and capital costs, central clearing and bilateral margin requirements are pushing collateral thresholds increasingly toward zero.

statement: Collateral thresholds are typically set equal to the initial margin.
explanation: Thresholds and initial margin work in opposite directions, so they are not seen together. Where initial margin is present, the threshold is typically zero.
originalText: Thresholds are typically set equal to the initial margin

statement: Counterparties agree to a non-zero (higher) threshold in a CSA mainly to reduce the operational workload and liquidity cost of margining, accepting some uncollateralised exposure.
explanation: A higher threshold means fewer and smaller margin calls, trading some risk mitigation for lower operational and liquidity costs.
originalText: To reduce the operational workload and liquidity cost of margining, accepting some uncollateralised exposure

statement: Counterparties agree to a non-zero (higher) threshold in a CSA to eliminate counterparty credit exposure entirely.
explanation: A higher threshold leaves more exposure uncollateralised, so it cannot eliminate counterparty credit exposure.
originalText: To eliminate counterparty credit exposure entirely

statement: Counterparties agree to a non-zero (higher) threshold in a CSA to increase the amount of collateral held against the current exposure.
explanation: A higher threshold reduces the collateral held, because margin is called only on exposure above it. Initial margin is what increases collateral.
originalText: To increase the amount of collateral held against the current exposure

statement: Under the regulatory margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, the initial margin amounts posted by the two parties may be netted against each other, so that only the net amount is exchanged.
explanation: Initial margin is exchanged by both parties on a gross basis. Each party posts its own amount and the two amounts cannot be offset.
originalText: Initial margin amounts posted by the two parties may be netted against each other, so that only the net amount is exchanged.
correction: Under the regulatory margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, the initial margin amounts posted by the two parties may not be netted against each other, so the gross amounts are exchanged.

changes.from: only the net amount is exchanged

statement: Under the regulatory margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, variation margin must be exchanged regularly (for example daily) with a zero threshold.
explanation: Variation margin is exchanged regularly and in full, without a threshold, unlike the thresholds common in ordinary CSAs.
originalText: Variation margin must be exchanged regularly (for example daily) with a zero threshold.

statement: Under the regulatory margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, initial margin may be calculated using validated internal models or regulatory tables, based on an extreme but plausible move over a 10-day horizon at a 99% confidence level.
explanation: Initial margin is calibrated to an extreme but plausible move over 10 days at 99% confidence, using either validated models or regulatory tables.
originalText: Initial margin may be calculated using validated internal models or regulatory tables, based on an extreme but plausible move over a 10‑day horizon at a 99% confidence level.

statement: In a collateral valuation dispute, if the disputed amount is under an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the counterparties may "split the difference"; otherwise, the cause of the difference must be found.
explanation: Splitting the difference is a shortcut reserved for small differences. Larger disputes require identifying the root cause and, if unresolved, obtaining market-maker quotes.
originalText: If the disputed amount is under an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the counterparties may “split the difference”; otherwise, the cause of the difference must be found.

statement: In a collateral valuation dispute, if the disputed amount is higher than an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the counterparties may "split the difference".
explanation: Splitting is for amounts below the acceptable level, not above it. Larger differences require finding the cause.
originalText: If the disputed amount is higher than an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the counterparties may “split the difference.”
correction: In a collateral valuation dispute, if the disputed amount is lower than an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the counterparties may "split the difference".

statement: In a collateral valuation dispute, if the disputed amount is under an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the parties should ignore it.
explanation: Small differences are not ignored. They are typically settled by splitting the difference.
originalText: If the disputed amount is under an acceptable level stated in the collateral agreement, the parties should ignore it; otherwise, the cause of the difference must be found.

statement: In reconciling a collateral dispute, the disputing party notifies the counterparty of its intent to dispute by the end of the day following the collateral call, transfers all undisputed amounts, and identifies the reason for the dispute.
explanation: These are the first two steps of the standard process. Quotes from market makers are requested only if the dispute remains unresolved.
originalText: Notify the counterparty of the intent to dispute by the end of the day following the collateral call, transfer all undisputed amounts, and identify the reason for the dispute.

statement: In reconciling a collateral dispute, the standard first step is to immediately request quotes from several market makers for the mark-to-market value of the disputed trades.
explanation: Market-maker quotes are the last step, used only for disputes that remain unresolved after the cause has been investigated.
originalText: Immediately request quotes from several market makers for the MtM value of the disputed trades and temporarily exclude the problematic assets from collateral calls.

statement: In reconciling a collateral dispute, the parties should split the difference on the disputed amount regardless of its size.
explanation: Splitting the difference is acceptable only when the difference is small. Larger differences stay uncollateralised until the cause is found and resolved.
originalText: Split the difference on the disputed amount regardless of its size to ensure a quick resolution and preserve the relationship.

statement: To resolve a collateral dispute that stems from different market data and closing times, the parties should review both valuation methodologies, market data sources and market closing times used for the disputed trades to identify the cause.
explanation: Market data and market close time are recognised sources of disputes. Standard practice is to transfer undisputed amounts and identify the reason for the dispute.
originalText: Review both parties’ valuation methodologies, market data sources and the market closing times used for the disputed trades to identify the cause.

statement: As a step in reconciling a collateral dispute, the disputing party notifies its counterparty (or the third-party valuation agent) that it disputes the exposure or collateral calculation.
explanation: Notification of the dispute is the first step of the process.
originalText: The disputing party notifies its counterparty (or the third‑party valuation agent) that it disputes the exposure or collateral calculation.

statement: As a step in reconciling a collateral dispute, the disputing party identifies the reason for the dispute and transfers the undisputed amount, and the parties attempt to resolve the dispute within a resolution time.
explanation: Transferring the undisputed amount and diagnosing the cause is the second step.
originalText: The disputing party identifies the reason for the dispute and transfers the undisputed amount, and the parties attempt to resolve the dispute within a resolution time.

statement: If the parties fail to resolve a collateral dispute within the resolution time, they obtain mark-to-market quotations from several market makers for the disputed components.
explanation: Quotes from several market makers are the final step for unresolved disputes.
originalText: If the parties fail to resolve the dispute within the resolution time, they obtain MtM quotations from several market makers for the disputed components.

statement: In reconciling a collateral dispute, both parties post collateral for the full amount of any disputed exposure, even if this means mutual overcollateralization.
explanation: Only undisputed amounts are transferred. The disputed exposure remains partly uncollateralised until the cause is traced and corrected.
originalText: Both parties post collateral for the full amount of any disputed exposure, even if this means mutual overcollateralization, so that neither counterparty is partially exposed during the dispute.

statement: Reconciling portfolios and valuations regularly, for example daily, and considering practice reconciliations before trading, reduces the chance of collateral disputes.
explanation: Frequent reconciliation aligns the parties' trade populations, valuations and margin requirements before a call is made, which prevents disputes rather than settling them.
originalText: Reconcile portfolios and valuations regularly, for example daily, and consider practice reconciliations before trading.

statement: Naming both counterparties as valuation agents, so that each can call for collateral on its own valuation, reduces the chance of collateral disputes.
explanation: Two valuation agents are used only when the counterparties are similar in size, and each calling on its own numbers can create disputes and processing delays.
originalText: Name both parties as valuation agents so each can call for collateral on its own valuation.

statement: The valuation agent is the party calling for delivery or return of collateral and so must handle all calculations: credit exposure, market value of posted collateral, uncollateralized exposure, and the delivery or return amount.
explanation: This is the standard list of valuation agent duties.
originalText: The valuation agent is the party calling for delivery or return of collateral and thus must handle all calculations, i.e., calculation of credit exposure, market value of posted collateral, uncollateralized exposure, and the delivery or return amount

statement: The threshold represents an amount of uncollateralized exposure: if an exposure is above the threshold, only the incremental exposure will be collateralized.
explanation: Exposure below the threshold is uncollateralised, and only the excess above it is collateralised.
originalText: The threshold represents an amount of uncollateralized exposure: if an exposure is above the threshold, only the incremental exposure will be collateralized

statement: An independent amount is effectively a negative threshold and is typically held as a cushion against gap risk, the risk that a transaction's market value may gap substantially and quickly.
explanation: The independent amount (initial margin) works in the opposite direction to the threshold and cushions gap risk.
originalText: An independent amount is effectively a negative threshold and is typically held as a cushion against ”gap risk”, i.e., the risk that a transaction’s market value may gap substantially and quickly

statement: A counterparty that posts a dividend-paying asset as collateral forfeits all dividends, because the receiver immediately becomes the economic owner of the collateral.
explanation: The collateral receiver is only a temporary holder and must pass dividends and coupons through to the giver. The giver keeps the economic benefits.
originalText: A counterparty who posts a dividend‑paying asset as collateral (i.e., the ”giver” of collateral) forfeits all dividends as the receiver immediately becomes the economic owner of the collateral

statement: In a bilateral collateral agreement, a party with positive mark-to-market calls for collateral from its counterparty, and a party with negative mark-to-market has its counterparty call for collateral from it.
explanation: Collateral flows from the party with negative MtM to the party with positive MtM, which is the party exposed to default.
originalText: If its MtM is positive it calls for collateral from the counterparty, and if its MtM is negative the counterparty calls for collateral from it.

statement: In a bilateral collateral agreement, a party with positive mark-to-market posts collateral, and a party with negative mark-to-market calls for collateral.
explanation: The flow is reversed: the party in the money is the one exposed to default and calls for collateral, while the party with negative MtM posts it.
originalText: If its MtM is positive it posts collateral, and if its MtM is negative it calls for collateral.

statement: Some smaller institutions prefer a longer margin call frequency because it gives them more time to meet operational and funding requirements.
explanation: A longer frequency reduces the operational and funding burden for institutions with limited capacity, at the cost of more uncollateralised exposure between calls.
originalText: a longer frequency gives them more time to meet operational and funding requirements.

statement: A longer margin call frequency removes the counterparty's uncollateralized exposure between calls.
explanation: A longer frequency increases the uncollateralised exposure between calls.
originalText: a longer frequency removes the counterparty’s uncollateralized exposure between calls.

statement: Typical collateralization agreements link thresholds and initial margins to counterparty credit rating, use tiered haircuts reflecting collateral riskiness, and pay interest on cash collateral at the overnight market rate.
explanation: Lower-rated counterparties get lower thresholds and larger initial margins, haircuts rise with collateral riskiness, and cash collateral earns the overnight rate.
originalText: Thresholds and initial margins linked to counterparty credit rating, tiered haircuts reflecting collateral riskiness, and interest on cash collateral at the overnight market rate.

statement: Sound haircut practice assigns higher haircuts to riskier assets such as equities and commodities, and low or zero haircuts to cash and high-quality government bonds.
explanation: Haircuts should scale with the collateral's volatility, liquidity and default risk.
originalText: Higher haircuts for riskier assets such as equities and commodities, and low or zero haircuts for cash and high‑quality government bonds.

statement: Applying a uniform 5% haircut across cash, government bonds and equities is consistent with sound haircut practice.
explanation: A uniform haircut penalises cash needlessly and understates the risk of equities. Haircuts should scale with the riskiness of the collateral.
originalText: A uniform 5% haircut across cash, government bonds and equities to simplify calculation.

statement: Applying no haircuts at all is consistent with sound haircut practice, because it encourages counterparties to post collateral.
explanation: Without haircuts the receiver is exposed to declines in the value of the collateral.
originalText: No haircuts at all, to encourage counterparties to post collateral.

statement: Collateral agreements typically tier the minimum transfer amount by credit rating, with higher MTAs for higher-rated counterparties and lower MTAs for weaker ones.
explanation: A larger MTA means more uncollateralised exposure, which is tolerable for strong credits. Weaker counterparties get lower MTAs to tighten mitigation where risk is greatest.
originalText: Tier the MTA by credit rating, with higher MTAs for higher‑rated counterparties and lower MTAs for weaker ones.

statement: Collateral agreements typically tier the minimum transfer amount by credit rating, with higher MTAs for lower-rated counterparties.
explanation: The tiering runs the other way: weaker counterparties get lower MTAs, not higher ones.
originalText: Tier the MTA by credit rating, with higher MTAs for lower‑rated counterparties.
correction: Collateral agreements typically tier the minimum transfer amount by credit rating, with higher MTAs for higher-rated counterparties.

statement: Following best practice, collateral posting should be continuous for both parties.
explanation: Margining is periodic, at least daily, to keep the operational workload under control. Continuous posting is not best practice.

statement: Variation margin is collateral that tracks the change in the mark-to-market of the position over time.
explanation: Variation margin follows the MtM of the position.
originalText: Variation margin is collateral that tracks the change in the MtM of the position over time.

statement: In a collateral agreement, the threshold and the minimum transfer amount are additive: exposure must exceed their sum before a call can be made.
explanation: A call requires the amount above the threshold to exceed the MTA, so exposure must exceed the threshold plus the MTA.
originalText: The threshold and the minimum transfer amount are additive: exposure must exceed their sum before a call can be made.

statement: Increasing the threshold in a collateral agreement increases the mitigation of exposure to counterparty default.
explanation: A higher threshold leaves more exposure uncollateralised and so reduces mitigation. A zero threshold means full collateralisation.
originalText: Increase the threshold
correction: Increasing the threshold in a collateral agreement reduces the mitigation of exposure to counterparty default.

statement: Increasing the independent amount in a collateral agreement increases the mitigation of exposure to counterparty default.
explanation: Initial margin adds overcollateralisation, which improves mitigation.
originalText: Increase the independent amount

statement: Decreasing the minimum transfer amount in a collateral agreement increases the mitigation of exposure to counterparty default.
explanation: A smaller MTA lets smaller exposures be collateralised.
originalText: Decrease the minimum transfer amount

statement: Increasing the margin call frequency, for example from weekly to daily, increases the mitigation of exposure to counterparty default.
explanation: More frequent calls reduce the unprotected exposure between calls.
originalText: Increase the margin call frequency (e.g., from weekly to daily)

statement: Higher initial margins protect against gap risk, the risk that a portfolio's value may gap substantially in a short period of time.
explanation: Initial margin is an extra cushion that stays in place even when variation margin lags, so it is sized to absorb large sudden movements in value if the counterparty defaults.
originalText: Higher initial margins

statement: Higher thresholds protect against gap risk, the risk that a portfolio's value may gap substantially in a short period of time.
explanation: A higher threshold increases the uncollateralised exposure below which no margin can be called, so it worsens gap risk.
originalText: Higher thresholds

statement: Higher minimum transfer amounts protect against gap risk, the risk that a portfolio's value may gap substantially in a short period of time.
explanation: A higher MTA delays small transfers and adds to residual uncollateralised exposure, so it weakens protection.
originalText: Higher minimum transfer amounts (MTA)

statement: Given funding and capital costs and the shift toward central clearing and bilateral margin requirements, thresholds in collateral agreements are increasingly zero.
explanation: Non-zero thresholds remain only for parties exempt from bilateral margin requirements, and central clearing requires full margining.
originalText: More zero thresholds

statement: Daily is the most common margin call frequency in OTC derivatives markets.
explanation: Daily margin calls are the standard in most OTC derivatives markets. Intraday calls are mainly for repos and cleared products.
originalText: Daily

statement: Weekly is the most common margin call frequency in OTC derivatives markets.
explanation: Weekly calls can be agreed with smaller or low-volatility counterparties, but daily calls are the norm.
originalText: Weekly
correction: Daily is the most common margin call frequency in OTC derivatives markets.

statement: When a downgrade trigger in a derivative contract is activated, the counterparty is required to post additional collateral, or the outstanding transactions may be terminated at market values.
explanation: A downgrade trigger gives the protected party additional collateral, or the right to close out at market value, as soon as credit quality falls below the agreed level.
originalText: The counterparty would be required to post additional collateral or potentially terminate outstanding transactions at market values.

statement: When a downgrade trigger in a derivative contract is activated, the counterparty is granted a grace period to improve its credit rating before any action is taken.
explanation: A trigger takes effect immediately. A grace period would defeat its purpose of protecting against rapid credit deterioration.
originalText: The counterparty would be granted a grace period to improve their credit rating before any action is taken.

statement: When a downgrade trigger in a derivative contract is activated, netting is suspended and the full gross value of all outstanding transactions becomes due immediately.
explanation: Netting remains in force. A trigger does not suspend it, and any close-out is at the net market value.
originalText: Netting will be suspended, and the full gross value of all outstanding transactions becomes due immediately.
